To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the application of ethnographic methods to the evaluation of co-design in healthcare settings requires an approach that is tailored to the specific context of the study and the needs of the participants.

the use of ethnography in the evaluation of healthcare quality improvement initiatives can provide a valuable insight into the process of change, but it requires a flexible, mixed-methods approach that is tailored to the context of the intervention.
ethnographic process evaluation can contribute to understanding of how quality improvement initiatives work in hospital settings.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the contribution of ethnography as a methodological approach to evaluating quality improvement in hospital services.
the contribution of ethnography in the evaluation of complex change in healthcare.
the use of ethnography to evaluate the process and impact of co-design projects within hospital settings, and the challenges of conducting ethnography within these contexts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

ethnography has a contribution to make to the evaluation of co-design and quality improvement in hospital contexts, but that this contribution must be carefully tailored to the context of the intervention and to the specific needs of the evaluation.
ethnography is not the most appropriate methodology for evaluating quality improvement in hospital-based settings.
ethnography is not a ‘silver bullet’ for evaluating quality improvement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of ethnography as a process evaluation tool is feasible and useful, particularly for quality improvement interventions in hospital settings.

the ethnographic process evaluation was successful in providing rich insights into the co-design process in two hospital settings, and that the approach taken was feasible and effective in providing an ethnographic account of quality improvement in the UK healthcare setting.

ethnographic evaluation can be used to provide rich, contextual insights into the process of quality improvement in busy hospital settings but requires a high level of engagement with participants and the setting to ensure that it remains sensitive to the complexity of clinical practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ethnography is not a ‘quick fix’ for evaluation, but it is an effective tool when applied with care, sensitivity and attention to the specificities of the context and setting.
the ethnographic approach is not a panacea for the evaluation of quality improvements in healthcare settings.

ethnography can contribute to the evaluation of co-design and quality improvement in busy hospital settings if the evaluation is conducted in close collaboration with participants and the wider context is considered.
